1. Is insufficient fleet capacity demons: NO. The dataset records citywide completed hourly rentals, not station inventory or failed rentals. Because 95% of all hourly demand across two years is under 563 rentals/hour, an illustrative fleet of 2,000 bikes is more than mathematically sufficient. The true problem is spatial-temporal misallocation.
2. How concentrated is hourly demand?: Extremely concentrated. The top 5 hours of the day generate 41.37% of total volume. On working days, 51.53% of all rentals occur in just the 6 peak commute hours.
3. What is the difference between commut: Registered riders represent 81.17% of total demand and drive predictable weekday commute peaks. Casual riders (18.83%) dominate weekend afternoons and are highly sensitive to weather conditions.
4. How does demand change across months?: Demand exhibits strong seasonal variation, peaking between May and October (summer/early autumn) and dropping by over 60% during winter months (January-February) due to temperature and precipitation.
5. What are the busiest operating period: Weekday mornings (08:00-09:00) and weekday evenings (17:00-18:00) during late spring through early autumn, where hourly system throughput frequently exceeds 600-800 rentals/hour.
6. How accurately can hourly demand be f: High accuracy. Gradient-boosted forecasting achieves an R² of 0.912 and an overall MAE of 42.0 rentals/hour on an untouched 6-month holdout test set.
7. How can forecasting improve operation: By providing 1- to 24-hour advance warning of expected demand surges, operations can dynamically stage rebalancing vans and schedule maintenance windows during low-demand night hours.
8. What additional data is needed for ac: Station-level dock occupancy (empty/full dock minutes), GPS trip origins and destinations, trip duration logs, failed unlock attempts (unmet demand), and rebalancing van relocation capacity.
